title: The pawn in a busy position
outcomes: Names the piece on a given square, and which way it moves, before using its rule
Taps every square a pawn can move to, including a pawn on its starting rank
Says that a pawn with a piece directly in front of it cannot move forward but may still capture diagonally
Says that an attacked square is still a legal destination for a pawn

steps.text: A pawn is the only piece that attacks different squares than it walks to. It walks straight and attacks at an angle. In a crowded position you must keep those two jobs apart. Watch the three boards, then try one yourself.

steps.caption: The pawn on e2 can capture the bishop on d3, because d3 is a forward diagonal with an enemy piece on it.

line.say: The pawn captures diagonally: it takes the bishop and now stands on d3.
Black replies with the knight. It was never attacked by the pawn on d3, which watches only c4 and e4.

steps.caption: The same pawn can capture the other way too: the knight on f3 stands on the other forward diagonal.

line.say: Capturing on the other side moves the pawn to the f-file for good.
Black makes a waiting move with the king.

steps.caption: Forward works differently. Both e3 and e4 are empty, so the pawn on its starting square may jump two.

line.say: Both squares ahead were empty, so the two-square jump is allowed.
The bishop can capture the pawn that jumped next to it.

steps.text: Before you look for squares, **name the piece** and check its colour. White pawns walk up the board and black pawns walk down. The rules are the same, only the direction flips. A common slip [H]: using White's direction for a black pawn. Check the colour every time.

steps.caption: White walks up, Black walks down. Two pawns on the same file therefore head toward each other.

line.say: White's pawn jumps up from its starting square.
Black's pawn jumps down. The two pawns now face each other.

steps.caption: Black to move. The pawn on d7 can capture the bishop on e6: its forward diagonals point down the board.

line.say: The black pawn captures downward and to the side, taking the bishop.

steps.caption: A black pawn that has already moved goes one square at a time. This one can step to d4 or capture on c4 or e4.

line.say: Black captures the rook. The pawn on e4 now attacks d3 and f3.

steps.text: Two things stop a pawn on the board. A piece directly ahead blocks the step, and the pawn cannot capture it, because pawns only capture diagonally. For the two-square jump, **both** squares must be empty. Your own pieces block just as enemy ones do. A third rule comes later: a pinned pawn may not move at all.

steps.caption: The knight on e5 blocks the pawn and cannot be captured, but the rook on d5 is on the diagonal.

line.say: The pawn cannot go forward, so it captures on the diagonal instead.
Black makes a waiting move.

steps.caption: Now your own pieces stand ahead and on the diagonal. The pawn has no move at all.
Black's own knight stands on d6 in front of the pawn, so the pawn cannot move either.
A preview, not yet taught: the bishop on h5 pins the pawn to its king. Both forward squares are empty, yet the pawn has no legal move.
The pawn is on its starting square but the bishop stands on d4. The jump is blocked; the single step is not.

line.say: Only d3 is free, so the pawn steps one square and now stands next to the bishop.

steps.caption: The knight stands on d3, directly in front. The pawn has no step and no jump.
One of your own pieces on the far square also stops the jump. The pawn can still take the single step.

line.say: The step to e3 is free, so the pawn walks one square.

steps.text: A pawn may step onto a square that an enemy piece attacks. An attacked square is one the enemy piece could capture on next. The step is legal; it may simply lose the pawn. Keep two questions apart: *can the pawn go there*, and *is it a good idea*. Here we answer only the first. Later lessons teach the second.

steps.caption: The rook on g3 attacks the square e3. Even so, the pawn may step there.

line.say: The step is legal because e3 is empty; an attack on the square does not change a pawn's basic movement.
The rook can capture the pawn next, so being legal is not the same as being safe.

steps.caption: The jump to e4 is also legal, and the rook does not attack e4. Same pawn, different consequence.

line.say: The pawn jumps two squares to a square the rook does not attack.
Black moves the rook to attack the pawn on e4 along the fourth rank.

steps.caption: A pawn also controls empty squares. The pawn on e2 attacks d3, so the black king may not step there, though nothing stands on d3 to capture.

steps.title: Blocked, free, distant
steps.prompt: Predict how many squares the pawn can reach in each position.

steps.caption: The question is which piece, not which rule. The pawn on d2 is stuck behind the black pawn, but the knight on b2 jumps over pieces and can capture d3.

line.say: The knight jumps to d3 and captures the pawn that blocked the white pawn.
Black makes a waiting move.

steps.caption: On the edge a pawn has only one diagonal. This pawn can step, jump, or capture the knight on g3.

line.say: The pawn captures the knight, leaving the edge for the g-file.

steps.caption: A real opening position, reached after 1.e4 d5. White's e-pawn can step forward or capture the black pawn.

line.say: The pawn takes diagonally.
Black can recapture with the queen. This is a line of the Scandinavian Defence [R].

steps.caption: Another real position (1.d4 d5 2.c4). Black's pawn on d5 is blocked by the white pawn ahead, so it cannot step to d4. The pawn on c4 stands on a diagonal.

line.say: Black captures on the diagonal, since the pawn cannot go forward.
3.e3 is one common reply, the Queen's Gambit Accepted [R].

steps.text: Pieces can retreat, but pawns cannot, so each pawn move changes the board for good [I]. Edward Lasker argued that the pawn skeleton is the lasting part of a position, so pawns should move only after thought. Philidor is quoted by Young: "The Pawns are the soul of Chess" (Chess Generalship).

[H] My guess: the pawn's odd rule (walks straight, attacks sideways) is what lets pawns form chains and walls, the skeleton the other pieces work around. [H] A second guess: most beginner pawn errors come from mixing the walking rule with the capturing rule. Which of the two do you mix up more often?

steps.caption: A walk-through for a new position. Step 1: name the piece. The piece on c2 is a white pawn, so it walks up the board.
Step 2: the forward question. c3 and c4 are both empty and the pawn is on its starting square.

line.say: Both squares were empty, so the jump is available.
Black makes a waiting move.

steps.caption: Step 3: the diagonal question. The black pawn on b3 can be captured. d3 is empty, so there is nothing to take there, though the pawn still attacks that square.

line.say: The pawn captures diagonally onto the enemy pawn.
The knight recaptures; the white pawn was attacked but it could still move.

steps.caption: Step 4: put both answers together. The pawn has exactly three moves, even though two enemy pieces attack it.

steps.text: Last task: teach it. Picture a pawn on e4 facing an enemy pawn on e5, then write your explanation for a friend.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend, in your own words, why the pawn on e4 facing a pawn on e5 cannot move, and what it could capture. Write it before you read the model answer.

steps.text: **Model answer.** Name the piece and its colour. The square ahead holds a piece, and a pawn never captures straight ahead, so it cannot step. It may capture only a piece on a square diagonally ahead; if both are empty, it has no move. An attacked square is still a legal square.

steps.prompt: Compare your explanation with the model. What did you leave out? In the unlabelled items, which question did you ask first, forward or diagonal?
